title: Diodes: I–V curves, rectifiers and a Zener regulator
goal: Trace a diode's I–V curve, turn AC into DC with a half-wave rectifier and a filter capacitor, and hold a voltage steady with a Zener diode.
theory: A silicon diode conducts once its forward voltage reaches about 0.6–0.7 V; the current then rises exponentially (Shockley: I = I_S·(e^(V/(n·V_T)) − 1)). In reverse only a tiny leakage flows — until breakdown.
Half-wave rectifier: the load sees the positive half-cycles minus one diode drop, so V_peak,out ≈ V_peak,in − V_D (the generator's 50 Ω takes a little more).
Add a capacitor across the load and it holds the peak between cycles. It sags by the ripple V_r ≈ V_peak,out / (f·R_L·C) before the next peak recharges it.

A Zener diode is built to break down at a set reverse voltage V_Z. Fed through a series resistor R_S, it keeps its node near V_Z while the extra current I_Z = (V_S − V_Z)/R_S − V_Z/R_L flows through it.

prelab.label: Peak output of the half-wave rectifier (5 V peak in, 0.7 V drop)
Ripple with R_L = 10 kΩ, C = 10 µF at 60 Hz
Zener current: 12 V, R_S = 470 Ω, V_Z = 5.1 V, R_L = 1 kΩ

procedure: Load the reference build. On the curve tracer (Bench → Curve tracer, mode diode) trace D3, a 1N4148: read V at 1 mA.
The generator gives a 10 Vpp, 60 Hz sine. CH1 shows the input (c10), CH2 the half-wave output across RL1 (column 16). Read the peak with the scope.
Move CH2 to the filtered output (column 22), switch CH2 to AC coupling and read the ripple Vpp.
Measure the Zener node (column 30) with the DMM. Change RZ (the load) to 470 Ω and 10 kΩ: the voltage hardly moves.
